Many have read Heidegger's remarks on our relations to things as saying that human beings are immersed in the world through language and everyday practices. This perspective suggests, on the one hand, that we cannot break through or extricate ourselves from our emplacement so as to get at things from the "outside," as it were, and, on the other hand, that the things of the world are never trumped by language or ideas. Our holistic entanglements are material and practical first and foremost. Hubert Dreyfus is a well-known proponent of this position and posits Heidegger as a "robust realist," meaning that Heidegger avoids the Scylla ofnaive realism and the Charybdis of idealism ("Coping" n.p.). The world is a participant in the ongoing event of human being-in-the-world, not a stage or backdrop to what human beings do and say. And this is a nuanced participation, with things emerging from and participating in human practices, and human practices in turn requiring things. Such an interpretation is fine as a first take, except that it exhibits a certain skewing: the nexus remains tethered to human being. Human usage and behavior become the privileged means of access to the background, and things, such as tools, light up to our awareness as we use them; then, when our attention shifts elsewhere, they dim back into the shadowy realm of equipment (Zeug) in general, the undifferentiated, always receding backdrop of"stuff."1 Heidegger certainly lends himself to such a reading. Speaking ofa room, he remarks that we encounter it not as a geometrical space but as "equipment for residingp that we have at least discovered, and that discovery and our activities yield

an arrangement that allows individual items to show themselves (BT 98). I take the steps downstairs into the basement, set out my books, organize my papers, boot the laptop, put some Klaus Schulze on the turntable, sit on the chair at the desk, insert the pen drive, enter words into the chapter file (i.e., write), read, take notes, edit, save the file, put on some Dexter Gordon. adjust the stereo volume, and so forth, with aspects of the room now near and now far from my attentions and activities. In various ways, these things all go together; there is an arrangement from which individual entities already derive their place wherefrom I can weave them through my activities. Entities in turn show up and dim back into the recesses as my attention flows variously through my purposeful activity.

In Tool-Being Graham Harman argues that such readings, reminiscent of Dreyfus, are not wrong but nevertheless miss something crucial to the nature of equipment and objects. Objects can no more be positioned solely within the horizon of human intention or awareness than language can. My example of the basement illustrates this tendency, since everything has its "nearness" and "farness" in relation to my attentions and intentions. One could of course add more history here and pile on thick description across the attentions and intentions of other people, social roles, and equipment. But none of this suffices to give us any ultimate grip on the object. Harman argues that "ifwe could total up all the 'contexts, roles, and social goals' in which a specific bridge or flagpole are currently embedded, this would still not give us the being of these objects" (TB 124). Any use or meaning that I or anyone else can bring, or even the plenitude of people, uses, contexts, histories, and other objects that could be brought forward, only serves to present some particular qualities out of the object's fulsomeness, or what Harman calls its "grand, dark abundance" (TB 125). Indeed. as the new wave of cognitive science (such as the work of Andy Clark, Paul Dourish, Anthony Chemero, and so on) demonstrates, the use of tools and local environmental scaffolding inspires changes in our sense of embodiment, blurring boundaries; to use a computer mouse, for instance, amounts to making that mouse part of one's body, and in so doing, it effectively disappears.8 Thus, predicating ontological distinctions on human attention and its shifting cognitive and bodily boundaries is fruitless; the ontological has to manifest beyond such human-derived loci, and thus withdrawal does not depend on human perception or any other singular interaction.

In all such partly verbal, partly nonverbal kinds of rhetorical devices, the nonverbal element also persuades by reason of its symbolic character. Paper need not know the meaning of fire in order to burn. But in the "idea" offire there is a persuasive ingredient. By this route something of the rhetorical motive comes to lurk in every "meaning" however purely "scientific" its pretensions. Wherever there is persuasion, there is rhetoric. And wherever there is "meaning," there is "persuasion." Food, eaten and digested, is not rhetorical. But in the meaning o[food there is much rhetoric, the meaning being persuasive enough for the idea of food to be used, like the ideas ofreligion, as a rhetorical device of statesmen. (RM 172-73)

This passage seems far from clear. Additionally, the numerous ironizing quotation marks and italics indicate various forms of pressure and stress. The word meaning, not insignificantly, is italicized twice and twice placed in quotation marks. What does meaning mean here? The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. Meaning is gleaned from the symbolicity that drapes over (or maybe permeates) the mundane world, circulating it as the significance available to us. The mention of science is important here, for Burke is clearly dissatisfied with a positivist, scientific claim of mere facticity for things of the world, as if measuring qualia sufficed for generating meaning. Thus, he will grant that paper, being paper, has no ideas as such; its rapid oxidation at temperatures around 451 degrees Fahrenheit is a purely chemical reaction. But to remain at this level is to willfully (or methodologically) remain at observation degree zero, and it obscures fire's role in human affairs. When Bradbury's Fireman comes to

burn the books, though, we move into a different realm, one of meaning, and we see that fire is a full rhetorical participant. Fire, then, is more than just a sensed material phenomenon; its integration into the human world necessitates ideas. These ideas mean, and insofar as they mean, they bodily invoke, and insofar as they bodily invoke, they persuade.

As I observed in my discussion of Hawhee, this is not an abstract notion of fire as meaningful; rather, it is one entirely grounded in the bodily integration of ideas stemming from physical experience. As Burke puts it in Attitudes toward History, "our primeval ancestors, by learning language, no longer experienced a sensation solely as a sensation" (382). As he goes on to explain, we may like the warmth ofa fire, and such warmth is certainly a sensation, but as soon as we start putting such experience into language, the words come to "tell a story"; as a result, attitudes (or affective stances) can emerge and be deployed across various forms of discursive interaction, such as the movement from "that feels warm" to the observation that someone is "warm-hearted" (Burke,AH383).

This elevation of meaning over mundane, objective matter is further evinced in other passages. Later in A Rhetoric of Motives Burke again discusses the effect of material phenomena. This time he calls them a form of intuition, and he then tethers intuition to a notion of infancy. One can perceive a seashell, for instance, and note the generative regularity of its spiral. but without more firmly and robustly grasping the intelligibility of that spiral in the world of human meaning, such as reasoning out the mathematical functions that generate various spirals, such an encounter remains stuck in what he terms "infancy," a notion he further compares to the "realm of the unconscious in dreams" (RM 174-75). But before we begin complaining about the terribly slanted and problematic valuation here, where conscious reason trumps infantile intuition, we must see the antistrophe he proposes immediately thereafter. An "intuition" of spring is not a mere passive perception, a datum of sensory (or even supersensory) knowledge. As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. Writing in the 1920s, the philosopher Martin Heidegger advanced a theory of emotion that is gaining credence today not only in the humanities but in the sciences (Ciborra, Ratcliffe, Gallagher and Schmicking, Wheeler). Heidegger's thoughts on emotion are, perhaps ironically, indebted to Aristotle's treatment of emotion in the Rhetoric, which Heidegger first addressed in his 1924 seminar Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy and then later built on for Being and Time. Heidegger points out that the theoretical attitude common to science and epistemology treats the emotions as psychical phenomena, which is to say, subjective experiences stemming from the world and tainting the possibility of impartial access. Certainly emotions do exist in this sense, and socialization in part entails learning to cope with, shape, and even control these emotional expressions. But other, more fundamental emotions elude such conscious apprehension and control. In a number of works, Heidegger argues for a form of emotion he calls Stimmung, customarily translated as "mood" or "attunement" (I will

use both, but overall I prefer "attunement" because it more clearly situates mood beyond the subjective and encompasses both the social and the material environments); he takes this form of emotion to be constitutive and not secondary for everyday human practices. Mood or attunement in this sense might be more akin to the rhythm of life. We cannot get to things as they "really are" divorced from mood because mood is a prerequisite for experiencing the world. Heidegger writes that we are always already attuned in our very grounds, so that there is "only ever a change of attunement [Stimmung]" (FCM 68). Mood is ontological; it takes form in the preintelligible background necessary for us to make sense of, experience, and interact in the world. As Heidegger states, "a mood [Stimmung] assails us. It comes neither from the 'outside' nor from the 'inside', but arises out of Being-in-the-world, as a way of such Being" (BT 176). Mood emerges from our involvements, acting as a kind of cradle from which the "how" of those involvements, their bearing and intensity, also emerges. Or to put this in a way that generatively resonates with ambience, Heidegger writes that an attunement is already there, "like an atmosphere in which we first immerse ourselves in each case and which then attunes us through and through" (FCM 67). This means that mood/attunement is not "inside" us, although neither is it simply exterior; rather, it is "the way of our being there with one another" (FCM 66).'3 For instance, depression as a mood conspicuously transforms how the world shows up for us; the listlessness common to depression is not just the experience of an already preexisting subject; rather, it transforms a person's world so that the world comes to take part in the depression. Depression generates a cut sundering afflicted persons from their ties to the world and other people, generating further separation that in turn exacerbates the depression. Depression, that is, is mood as attunement in that it permeates the entire situation, not simply the interior mental state of the person, which is one reason that overcoming it requires more than an act ofwill.14

Recent neurocognitive research into emotion lends empirical support to Heidegger's thinking. Antonio Damasio, for instance, postulates three levels of emotion, with the third, "background feeling," being comparable to Heidegger's Stimmung. Damasio describes it (fortuitously, in musical terms) as "minimalist in tone and beat, the feeling oflife itself, the sense of being" (Descartes' 150; see also Feeling 52-53). Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

A number of contemporary studies have attempted to bring more theoretical precision to the concept of ambience, many doing so by resuscitating the more active, embracing connotations of the Greek periechon. These contemporary attempts characteristically emphasize ambience's role in perception, as when Jean-Paul Thibaud says that "ambience puts us in immediate contact with a situation in its entirety" (2). Such an approach rejects the notion of situations as mere composites of what is subjectively requisite, or the intersection of networking strands, with everything else relegated to epiphenomena, and instead sees a11 elements as operational and even necessary, albeit at various levels of scale. But not all these elements are oriented on the perceiving subject, making ambience transubjective, hence the necessity for an ecological conception of the perceptual environment in which various levels of attention and attunement are in play. Thibaud further remarks that ambience situates us in a "certain bodily and emotive disposition" that is experienced, meaning, importantly, that ambience cannot be reduced to interpretative acts; it is a "diffuse, disseminated presence" not reducible to the salience we customarily seek through interpretation and analysis (4). In this way, ambience is given a more vital quality; it is not an impartial medium but an ensemble of variables, forces, and elements that shape things in ways difficult to quantify or specify. These elements are simultaneously present and withdrawn, active and reactive, and complexly interactive among themselves as much as with human beings. Indeed, as Thibaud argues via J. J. Gibson, on this count human perception is not solely human doing, since it requires activity that re-

sponds to and depends on the external environs being perceived (Thibaud 8).1 address these issues more extensively in chapters 5 and 6.

Indeed, to give an example that bridges the millennia. we can compare the designed use of Lascaux as afforded by its spatial, acoustic, and material properties to musicians' attempts to get a certain sound by recording in a specific environment. For instance, some of John Bonham's most famous drum sounds on Led Zeppelin albums-reputedly the most sampled drums in the digital age-were achieved using specific recording techniques in suitable places, such as the former poorhouse Headley Grange, in East Hampshire. England. Such sound-the "sound of sound," as it were-was achieved by making the environs integral to the recording process. In songs such as Led Zeppelin IV's "When the Levee Breaks," the recording captured not just Bonham playing the drums or just the drums responding to the room but the room responding to the drums (E. Davis 74). 6 We understand that recording technology is artfully deployed to capture not an isolated drum sound or just a drum sound as perfected through Bonham's considerable technique but a sound's ambient fulfillment in an environment that brings its own unique qualities. In another environment, other qualities emerge, and even with the same drums and drummer in the same band, a different sound will result. Thus, despite the differences in technologies and purposes. in principle the ambient songs at Lascaux and Headley Grange remain the same.

While perception remains important to understanding ambience, other important aspects include feeling, mood, intuition, and decision making. This gets us to the issue of attunement. That is, ambience involves more than just the whole person, as it were; ambience is inseparable from the person in the environment that gives rise to ambience. There is no person who can then be tacked onto the environment. Attunement is not additive. Rather, there is a fundamental entanglement, with the individuation of particular facets being an achieved disclosure. Thus, wakefulness to ambience is not a subjective achievement but rather an ambient occurrence: an attunement. It is always ongoing, and achievement of some sense of harmony or synchronicity would, on this account, be fleeting. My arguments for the importance of ambience should not be understood as any simple call to "pay attention." One is in any event only partially aware of ongoing events within one's environs at any given time. The environs are ready-to-hand, yes, but they now have agentive powers Heidegger's hammer never had. Emile A arts and Stefano Marzano point out, "As technology becomes hidden within these static, unintelligent objects, they will become subjects, active and intelligent actors in our environment ... [and the] immaterial world of our interactions with them-services, games, entertainment, information, communication-will become more prominent in our lives" (8-9). Greenfield argues that ubiquitous computing "will disturb unwritten agreements about workspace and homespace, the presentation of self and the right to privacy. It contains an inherent, unsettling potential for panoptical surveillance, regulation, and 'rationalization.' Its presence in our lives will transfigure our notions of space and time, self and other, citizen and society in ways we haven't begun to contemplate" (3). In short, ambient intelligence radically changes who we are in our environs; it

situates us differently in the world, evoking other ways of being. It thereby also reveals rhetoric to us differently than it has appeared heretofore. Ambience thus teaches us that we cannot rely solely on salience, attention, and consciousness to guide us.

Rhetoric has much to learn from music on this score. I am claiming that ambient music is an important development, both in its own right as a form of thinking (and not simply as expression ofhuman thought and affect) and as something that shows how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to the music's creation but to what we take the music to be. Music is not just the salience of its affective work. Ambient music has still other rhetorical dimensions, including politics. It has ramifications for how we dwell in the world. Eno claims that ambient music is directly political: "The decision to stop seeing yourself as the centre of the world, to see yourself as part of the greater flow of things, as having limited options and responsibility for your actions[.] ... that is political theory: and it's where the music grows from" (qtd. in Tamm 91).

It is hardly a stretch to see that these political insights resonate with the extension of digital computing into things and environs. As Eno is quite aware, there are both opportunities and dangers here, which is why transforming how one sees oneself in the world is integral to a politics attuned to these dangers. 21 So, much as ambient music does, ubiquitous computing (ambient intelligence) showcases how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to our everyday activity but to a conception of dynamic life itself. We need not overstate the case by claiming we are on the threshold of a brave new world. Rather, we are simply seeing capacities, implications, and energies as previously assembled now giving way to vibrant and different intensities and assemblages. But we cannot ignore how these different forms also assemble new forms oflife, or new ways of being-in-the-world.

Rhetoric, Ambience, Dwelling

We need conceptions ofrhetoric that keep pace with these transformations and their attendant opportunities and dangers, that not only help us make sense of them but enable us to flourish (and that will, of course, spur new transformations). We do not need a new rhetoric, however; rather, we must work anew with what has been brought forward in rhetorical theory and practice. Rhetoric is revealing and doing-doing as revealing and revealing as doing-and hence integral to our dwelling in the world. There is thus another dimension to persuasion that is as fundamental as the issue Davis hosts for us. Sociality resides. It is always somewhere, and this somewhere can never be fully circumscribed by either meaning or symbolicity. We are worldly. Necessarily, our a priori affectability is not just a transaction among animate beings-humans primarily, but as Davis suggests, also nonhuman animals-so that we see this affectability as enmeshed in material locales that give place and bearing prior to symbolicity proper. All being must be part of the giving of what gives, and the world is what is given, both as meaning and as what withdraws from meaning, even ifworld is not equivalently given. Thus, the challenge of this chapter is to think how rhetoric is caught up in the play of language and materiality while raising the specter that neither language nor materiality can be reduced to symbolicity. Indeed, that is the problem: to what extent can we discuss materiality prior to meaning or symbolicity, and how can we discuss what gives rise to symbolicity as part of symbolicity itself? These questions are themselves problematic from Burke's perspective. Burke almost uniformly places meaning first, and the rhetoricity implicit to symbolic action emerges with it. Heidegger, too, can be and frequently has been read as offering this position, which thus has been taken to mean that world, while certainly material, is always already and only one of significance, making

world inseparable from meaning. I, however, am going to argue that while the world is a world of involvements, and hence meaning, world is also involved in those involvements in ways that are never captured, submerged, or rendered secondary to world as it emerges for human being. This sense of world requires a rich materiality that bears up and stays within human sociality and significance, so that it must also be understood as constituting affective relationality, without, for all that, collapsing into human sociality and significance. Such materiality, as I will show in the upcoming chapters, should always be understood across the play of presence and withdrawal, and human being is only one locus for this play.

When I claim rhetoric is ontological, then, I mean that (1) we come to see that rhetoric cannot be sundered from material being or reduced to epistemological considerations; (2) we understand that rhetoric is intimate with the environments in which it emerges (and not just to which it is joined, as in two separate realms coming together), which grants non humans an elemental role in rhetoricity; (3) this intimacy is not solely a matter of human projection, control. or assignment; and (4) grappling with these entangled, mutually coevolving, and transformative interactions among persons, world, and discourses requires a new appreciation for their constitutive complexity. I can reduce this to a somewhat more succinct statement: rhetoric is a responsive way of revealing the world for others, responding to and put forth through affective, symbolic, and material means, so as to (at least potentially) reattune or otherwise transform how others inhabit the world to an extent that calls for some action (which can include, of course, steadfastness, refusal, or even apathy). Beyond resonating with Davis's approach, my line of thought also bears an affinity to George Kennedy's important essay "A Hoot in the Dark," where Kennedy claims that rhetoric is energy (2). I augment Kennedy, however, by adding that energy is always materialized. Energy emerges within and transforms how one dwells in the world or at least allows for that world to show up, to reveal itself, differently. Ifwe are going to keep to persuasion, then, this is a further intensification of it. Persuasion thought ambiently looks to a materialist affectability that sustains our being-in-the-world. An ambient rhetoric will have taken things at their world and notjust their word.
